1 Load data

SNEUCX_train <- read_rds("input/SNEUCX_train.rds")
source("functions/testdf.R")

2 Mean equation

2.1 ACF and PACF of log returns

Code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
acf(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,
    lag.max = 36,
    lwd = 5, 
    col = "red", 
    main = "ACF",
    xlim = c(2,36),
    ylim = c(-0.1,0.1))

Code 
pacf(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,
     lag.max = 36,
     lwd = 5, 
     col = "red", 
     main = "PACF",
     xlim = c(2,36),
     ylim = c(-0.1,0.1))

Code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

ACF and PACF plots show that 7th and 10th lags are significant. This suggest analizing model ARMA up to order 10 of p and q.

2.2 Mean equation model

We will choose models based on BIC criterion as it penalizes large number of parameters the most. We prefer parsimonious models that won’t over fit. We fit models with p up to 10 and q up to 10. Some models will be defined manually as auto.arima doesn’t take into consideration models, that have only for example 10th lag without lags from 1 to 9.

Code 
Akaike <-c()
Bayes <-c()

arma10_10 <- Arima(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,
                  order = c(10, 0, 10),
                  fixed = c(0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,NA,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,NA,NA)
                  )
Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,AIC(arma10_10))
Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,BIC(arma10_10))

arma7_10_7_10 <- Arima(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,
                  order = c(10, 0, 10),
                  fixed = c(0,0,0,0,0,0,NA,0,0,NA,0,0,0,0,0,0,NA,0,0,NA,NA)
                  )
Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,AIC(arma7_10_7_10))
Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,BIC(arma7_10_7_10))

arma0_7 <- Arima(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,
                  order = c(0, 0, 7),
                 fixed = c(0,0,0,0,0,0,NA,NA)
                  )
Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,AIC(arma0_7))
Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,BIC(arma0_7))

arma7_0 <- Arima(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,
                  order = c(7, 0, 0),
                 fixed = c(0,0,0,0,0,0,NA,NA)
                  )
Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,AIC(arma7_0))
Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,BIC(arma7_0))

arma1_0 <- Arima(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,
                  order = c(1, 0, 0)
                  )
Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,AIC(arma1_0))
Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,BIC(arma1_0))

arma0_1 <- Arima(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,
                  order = c(0, 0, 1)
                  )
Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,AIC(arma1_0))
Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,BIC(arma1_0))

arma0_0 <- Arima(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,
                  order = c(0, 0, 0)
                  )

Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,AIC(arma0_0))
Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,BIC(arma0_0))

Series: SNEUCX_train$LnReturns 
ARIMA(0,0,0) with zero mean 

sigma^2 = 0.0003605:  log likelihood = 2562.82
AIC=-5123.64   AICc=-5123.64   BIC=-5118.73

ACF and PACF plots shows us that adding 10th lag to ma and ar equation removes statistically significant 10th lag and 7th lag remains borderline significant. ARMA with only 7th lag in AR or 7th lag in MA still shows 10th significant lag in PACF or ACF.

Auto arima function proposes ARMA00 or so called naive model.

Code 
model_name <- c("arma10_10","arma7_10_7_10","arma0_7","arma7_0", "arma1_0","arma0_1","arma0_0")

scores <- cbind(model_name, Akaike, Bayes)
colnames(scores) <- c("Model","Akaike","Bayes")

scores %>% 
  datatable(rownames = FALSE, class = 'cell-border stripe') %>% 
  formatRound(columns = c("Akaike","Bayes"), digits = 0)

Manually created models compared to “no model” perform worse in terms of BIC score. In that case we will continue with ARIMA(0,0,0)

2.3 Stationarity testing

Code 
testdf(variable = arma0_0$residuals,
       max.augmentations = 3) %>% 
  datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = 't', ordering=F), class = 'cell-border stripe') %>% 
  formatRound(columns = c('adf', 'p_adf', 'bgodfrey', 'p_bg'), digits = 4)

Based on Breusch Godfrey test we can not reject hypothesis that there is no autocorrelation among residuals for DF test with 0 augmentations. P-value for ADF test with zero augmentations is low - we can reject hypothesis that time series is non stationary. Residuals of ARIMA(0,0) is stationary.

3 ARCH effect

3.1 Serial autocorrelation

Code 
acf(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns^2,
    lag.max = 36,
    lwd = 5, 
    col = "red", 
    main = "ACF of squared log returns",
    xlim = c(2,36),
    ylim = c(-0.05,0.2))

Based on ACF on squared log returns/residuals of ARMA(0,0) we can see that serial autocorrelation is present which suggest ARCH effects.

3.2 ARCH test

Code 
arma0_0 <- arima(SNEUCX_train$LnReturns,order = c(0,0,0))
arch.test(arma0_0)
ARCH heteroscedasticity test for residuals 
alternative: heteroscedastic 

Portmanteau-Q test: 
     order   PQ    p.value
[1,]     4 24.9 0.00005263
[2,]     8 37.7 0.00000847
[3,]    12 41.2 0.00004607
[4,]    16 42.4 0.00034031
[5,]    20 43.9 0.00153346
[6,]    24 65.2 0.00001123
Lagrange-Multiplier test: 
     order   LM p.value
[1,]     4 2142       0
[2,]     8  981       0
[3,]    12  630       0
[4,]    16  464       0
[5,]    20  367       0
[6,]    24  259       0

Formally testing time series with ARCH LM test we can reject null hypothesis that ARCH effect is not present. In Portmanteau-Q test and Lagrange-Multiplier test we are rejecting null hypothesis indicating there is autocorrelation in squared residuals.

4 ARCH models

4.1 ARCH(1)

Code 
spec <- ugarchspec(variance.model = list(garchOrder = c(1,0)), mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0)))
ARCH1 <- ugarchfit(spec = spec, data = SNEUCX_train$LnReturns, solver = "hybrid")
print(ARCH1)

In optimal parameter section we can see that all parameters are statistically significant except for mu - mean parameter, alpha1 becomes less significant if we take into consideration robust standard errors.

Weighted Ljung-Box test on Standardized Residuals tells us that mean equation seems to be correct as we don’t have any significant autocorrelations.

Based on Weighted Ljung-Box Test on Standardized Squared Residuals, we can notice that fifth lag is still significant suggesting that variance equation may be enhanced.

We cannot reject the hypothesis that ARCH effects is not present based on 2, 4 and 6th lag.

Nyblom stability test suggest that jointly model is not stable - statistic is greater than 10% critical value, if we look at this individually omega is likely to change in time.

Additionally we reject the hypothesis that leverage effect exists.

ACF plot of standardized residuals shows significant autocorrelation for 7th and 10th lag.

ACF plot of squared standardized residuals shows significant autocorrelation for 5th lag. We will add up to 5th lag of innovation to next model.

Based on Adjusted Pearson Goodness-of-Fit Test we can see that normal distribution does not fit the data.

Standardized residuals don’t have normal distribution.

Finally model seems to be correct in terms of autocorrelation of standardized squared residuals and arch effects. Autocorrelation based on ACF plot and Ljung-Box test are no longer significant. Additionally, investigating ACF plot of standardized residuals we can see that none of lags up. to 15th have statistically significant autocorrelation. ARCH of order 9 is quite a lot, we will try fitting ARCH models of order 1 to 9 without such detailed analysis.

4.4 Aditional models

We will consider all ARCH models of order 1 to 9.

Code 
arch <-c()
for (i in 1:9){
  spec <- ugarchspec(variance.model = list(garchOrder = c(i,0)), mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0)))
  arch_tmp <- ugarchfit(spec = spec, data = SNEUCX_train$LnReturns, solver = "hybrid")
  arch <- cbind(arch,arch_tmp)
}

Looking at the first table with optimal parameters we can see that now all parameters are statistically significant except for mu in mean equation.

Ljung-box test on Standardized Residuals and the squared ones shows no autocorrelation within the residuals.

Based on Weighted ARCH LM test, ARCH effects are not present.

Nyblom stability test tells us that model parameters are jointly unstable, but looking at it individually, only omega is likely to change in time.

We reject the hypothesis that leverage effect is present.

ACF plot of standardized residuals and standardized squared residuals shows no significant serial autocorrelation up to 20th lag.

Based on Adjusted Pearson Goodness-of-Fit Test we can see that normal distribution does not fit the data, we will try with different distributions. By looking at qq plot we can see that marginal values lay significantly below/above solid line implying heavy tails.

As leverage effect is present we will additionally try fitting EGARCH and APARCH (recommended in documentation) models which takes this issue into account. Since for all Jarque-Bera tests null hypothesis about normal distribution among standardized residuals was rejected, we will try working with distributions such as t-student, skewed t-student, generalized error, skewed generalized error, skewed normal.

As an addition we will fit GARCH-in-Mean model, to see if including risk premium will enhance our model.

Code 
garch_models = c("sGARCH","eGARCH","apARCH")
distirbution = c("norm","std","sstd","ged","sged","snorm")
order_p = c(1,2)
order_q = c(1,2)

model_name <- c()
Akaike <-c()
Bayes <-c()
Shibata <-c()
HQ <-c()

for (i in 1:length(garch_models)){
  for (j in 1:length(distirbution)){
    for (k in 1:length(order_p)){
      for (l in 1:length(order_q)){
        
        spec <- ugarchspec(variance.model = list(garchOrder = c(order_p[k],order_q[l]),
          model = garch_models[i]),
          mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0)),
          distribution.model = distirbution[j])
        
        GARCH <- ugarchfit(spec = spec, data = SNEUCX_train$LnReturns, solver = "hybrid")
        model_name <- rbind(model_name,paste0(garch_models[i],"_",distirbution[j],"_",order_p[k],order_q[l]))
        if (is.null(GARCH)) {
          Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,NaN)
          Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,NaN)
          Shibata <- rbind(Shibata,NaN)
          HQ <- rbind(HQ,NaN)
        } else {
          Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,infocriteria(GARCH)[1])
          Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,infocriteria(GARCH)[2])
          Shibata <- rbind(Shibata,infocriteria(GARCH)[3])
          HQ <- rbind(HQ,infocriteria(GARCH)[4])
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

for (i in 1:length(garch_models)){
  for (j in 1:length(distirbution)){

6 Summary of information criteria for models

Code 
for (i in 1:length(arch)){
  model_name <- rbind(model_name,paste0("ARCH",i))
  Akaike <- rbind(Akaike,infocriteria(arch[[i]])[1])
  Bayes <- rbind(Bayes,infocriteria(arch[[i]])[2])
  Shibata <- rbind(Shibata,infocriteria(arch[[i]])[3])
  HQ <- rbind(HQ,infocriteria(arch[[i]])[4])
}

scores <- cbind(model_name, Akaike, Bayes, Shibata, HQ)
colnames(scores) <- c("Model","Akaike","Bayes","Shibata","Hannan-Quinn")

scores %>% 
  datatable(rownames = FALSE, class = 'cell-border stripe') %>% 
  formatRound(columns = c("Akaike","Bayes","Shibata","Hannan-Quinn"), digits = 4)

We can see that best performing models in terms of BIC scores are with t-student distribution.

We will choose models based on Bayes information criterion, two models with the lowest scores are:

  • standard GARCH with t-student distribution of order (1,1)

  • exponential GARCH with t-student distribution of order (1,1).

If we consider Akaike and Shibata scores, the second best model is

  • asymmetric power ARCH model with t-student distribution or order (1,1)

We will use this models for VAR modeling in later steps. Additionally we will include

  • standard GARCH-in-Mean model with t-student distribution of order (1,1)

for research purposes.

Optimal parameters:

  • all the parameters are significant except for mu and archm. Positive archm parameter indicates that there is risk premium but this parameter is statistically insignificant.

LB test:

  • no serial autocorrelation in standardized residuals - correct mean equation

  • no serial autocorrelation in standardized squared residuals - correct variance equation

ARCH LM test:

  • no ARCH effects

Nyblom stability test:

  • jointly model is not stable

  • individually omega, alpha1, beta1 and shape are not significant.

Sign bias test:

  • there is no leverage effect

Goodness-of-fit:

  • t-Student distribution fits the data distribution

Based on ACF of standardized residuals none of lags until 23 is autocorrelated, based on ACF on squared standardized residuals variance model is correct - no significant autocorrelation until 21 lag. News impact curve shows us that the impact of innovation on volatility is symmetric. QQ plot seems to be correct t-distribution matches data distribution.
